steps.title: Two people in a small orange boat
steps.html:
Reading 1 · 146 words

In the photograph two people are sitting on what looks like a small yellow and orange rubber boat, holding a real wooden paddle. It appears that the boat is being swept down a wild river towards a waterfall.

It is a wall. The boat is a large decorative painting on the side of a building in a quiet residential street, and the two people are standing in front of it on solid ground, holding a borrowed paddle at the angle the painting requires.

What makes it work is not the painting, which is competent rather than brilliant. It is the paddle. The eye accepts a flat surface as a scene the moment one real three-dimensional object is placed correctly inside it.

The photographer's own description is worth quoting: the hardest part, she said, was persuading two adults to sit on nothing in a public street with a straight face.

steps.title: Why your eyes agree to it
steps.html:
Reading 2 · 145 words

An illusion is not a failure of the eye. The eye reports light accurately. What happens next is that the brain, which has no direct access to the world, works out the most probable explanation for that light and shows you the answer rather than the working.

This is normally an advantage. A sharp shadow across a smooth surface is read as a shadow, not as a dark stripe, because in almost every case it is one.

The illusion works by placing the brain in a situation where the most probable answer is wrong. The half-submerged boat, the twinkling water, the impossible angle: each is individually plausible, and together they are enough.

This is why knowing that a picture is an illusion does not dissolve it. You can walk up to the wall, put your hand on it, and the boat is still there when you step back.

steps.title: Opinion first, then the facts, in a fixed order
steps.html:
The sequence English uses without ever being taught it.

When two or more adjectives come before a noun, English puts them in a fixed order, and reversing it sounds wrong even to speakers who could not explain why.

The order is: opinion – size – age – shape – colour – origin – material – purpose – NOUN.

a beautiful (opinion) little (size) old (age) round (shape) brown (colour) Italian (origin) wooden (material) serving (purpose) bowl. Nobody writes all eight, but that is the sequence they follow.

From the text: a small yellow and orange rubber boat — size, colour, material. a large decorative painting — size, purpose. a real wooden paddle — opinion-ish, material.

Two practical rules. Opinion always comes first: a lovely old house, never an old lovely house. And material and purpose always come last, next to the noun: a leather driving glove.

Commas: use them between adjectives of the same type (a cold, wet, miserable morning) and not between different types (a small orange rubber boat). And appears mainly between colours: yellow and orange.

steps.title: Putting four adjectives in order
steps.html:
1. The noun is boat, and the adjectives are: rubber, small, orange, ridiculous.
  2. Sort them by type. Ridiculous = opinion. Small = size. Orange = colour. Rubber = material.
  3. Put them in the sequence: opinion, size, colour, material. a ridiculous small orange rubber boat.
  4. Check the punctuation. All four are different types, so no commas.
  5. Now change one: if you had orange and yellow, both colours, you would join them with and: a small yellow and orange rubber boat — which is what the text says.

options.label: A painted wall or a mural where you live
A place that looks different from the street than it is inside

steps.title: Write your description.
steps.sub: 140–170 words. Describe what it appears to be, then what it is. Use at least four noun phrases with two or more adjectives, in the right order.
steps.html:
• Describe what it appears to be, using stacked adjectives.
  • Say what it actually is.
  • Say what makes it work — usually one detail.
  • Close with the fact that knowing does not help.

Useful language

  • At first it looks like a … … … .
  • It appears that … is about to …
  • In fact it is a large … … .
  • What makes it work is not … but …
  • Walking up to it reveals …
  • Knowing does not help: it is still there when you step back.
steps.modelHtml:
The window on Bukhar Zhyrau

From the far pavement it looks like a tall narrow lit window on the second floor, with a heavy dark green curtain half drawn across it and a small white cat sitting on the sill.

There is no window. The whole thing is painted onto a flat concrete panel that was put up when the building was renovated, and the light is a single bulb behind a piece of frosted plastic set into the wall.

What makes it work is not the painting, which is quite rough close up. It is the bulb. One real light source is enough to persuade the eye that everything around it has depth.

I have known about it for four years. It still looks like a window every time I come round the corner.
